vintage-reselling-1: A vintage reseller buys older goods for less than a buyer will pay, prepares them, sells them and ships them, and the money is in the gap after every cost. Margin and markup are not the same thing: margin is profit as a share of the price, and markup is profit as a share of the cost. I counted carriage, breakage and failed firings as costs, and you should list every cost of one item, not only what you paid. Work out the true profit on one item before you read on.

Selling a few of your own things is not running a business, and the line is drawn by indicators the authorities publish. Look at how often you sell, whether you buy to sell, and how you present yourself. Write which indicators apply to you today. A returns promise is part of how you sell, and a trader's promises are held to a standard.

Being a trader changes four things: your duties to buyers, your tax position, your platform account, and what the platform reports. Read each as a list of records to keep. I offered guarantees and free delivery as part of how I sold, and a trader's promises need a plan behind them. Write the four changes and a task for each.
vintage-reselling-2: Every sourcing channel trades price against effort, risk and volume. Compare charity shops, car boots, auctions and house clearances on those three. I varied one thing at a time and recorded the result, so test two channels with five items each and compare sell-through and profit. Where the law gives you fewer rights as a buyer, as at auction, buy at your own risk and price the risk in.

The only price that matters is what you can sell for after costs, less the profit you need. Estimate the sale price from sold items, take off the fees, postage and packaging, and set a walk-away rule. Do the arithmetic before you bid. The cheaper carriage rate can cost more once breakage is counted, so count breakage too.

Stock that does not sell is money you cannot spend. Set a budget and a category, check an item before you buy it, and log what you buy and how fast it sells. I tried a small number of things and wrote down the results, and the log is your trial. Repeat the test before you change the plan, because small samples mislead.
vintage-reselling-3: To say an item is vintage you need a reason a buyer could check. Build a date range from evidence of different strengths: marks and documents are strong, style is medium, a story is weak. I named styles and designs in my book, and a resemblance proves nothing about the maker. Write your evidence for one item and give it a strength. Say 'in the style of' unless you have more.

A buyer cannot touch the item, so your words and photographs are the product. Grade the condition with one scale, and disclose every flaw. Clean carefully and say what you did. I specified dimensions and showed the details at large, and you should measure and photograph close up. Write a description with every flaw and every measurement.

Brands and makers add value, so they also attract copies and wishful thinking. Describe what the item says, not what you hope it is. Run a short authenticity routine, and when you cannot answer, say 'I don't know' and leave the claim out. I counted the samples that failed and said how sure my test was; do the same, and word the listing to match what you found.
vintage-reselling-4: Older stock is where reselling meets the criminal law most often. Ivory and precious metals have strict rules, and an item that might be ivory should not be listed until it is confirmed. Hallmarks and weights matter for gold, silver, platinum and palladium. I tested a claim before I made it, and so should you: write the test, the result and the wording. When you cannot test, do not claim.

Older goods were made to older safety standards, and some cannot lawfully be sold by a business today. Check upholstered furniture for its fire labels, and electrical goods for a safe plug and cable. Check the other categories with strict rules. A competent person must test an electrical item before you say it works. Say 'untested, for display or parts' when you cannot test.

A trader selling to a consumer has duties on description, quality, delivery information and cancellation. The goods must match your description. Distance sales carry cancellation rights. Write a returns policy that fits the law. I showed my results with their figures and said how sure I was, and a listing that says what you know and do not know protects both you and the buyer.
vintage-reselling-5: Each platform sends you a different buyer and takes a different cut. Compare them using their own published fee pages, with the date you read them. Think from the customer's side: where would they look for this item? I treated the window as a craft, and the platform is your window. Write a table of three platforms and what each would cost you for one item.

A listing is a promise, and it sells the item and sets expectations at the same time. Photograph from every side, close up on flaws, with something for scale. Write a title and description in a fixed order, and remove every claim you cannot show. Exaggeration is dangerous, and a statement the buyer can check is worth more than a large one.

Price to the market and the ceiling, then measure what you keep. Work out the real profit per item and per hour, including fees, postage, packaging and time. Keep a table of percentages: views, sales, returns. Check the numbers twice. Plan a markdown for items that do not sell, and decide the date in advance.
vintage-reselling-6: Vintage goods are often fragile, awkward or heavy, so shipping decides many of your margins. Pack for the journey and price the postage from the real parcel. Weigh and measure each one. I took the inventory in one day and posted every entry twice, and a packing record works the same way: write the weight, the size and the cost. Keep what the carrier gave you as proof.

Some buyers will ask for returns. A calm, evidence-based process keeps the cost low. Keep your photographs and your description, and offer a fair remedy. Reduce returns by describing accurately in the first place. Record each dispute, the evidence and the outcome. If the totals do not agree, find the mistake.

Keeping records is how you pay the right amount of tax and prove it. Know when tax and filing begin, and compare the trading allowance with your actual expenses by working the numbers both ways. Know what platforms report about you. Close your stock count each week, and keep a ledger whose two sides agree. When they disagree, there is an error to find.
vintage-reselling-cap: The capstone is a launch pack for your first five items. It joins all six modules in one document. Take the inventory of the five in one day, record each purchase with the date and the terms, and work a price ceiling and profit for each. Check each item against the restricted-goods and safety gates. Write the pack so that a stranger could follow it.

Review the pack as a buyer, a Trading Standards officer and a tax inspector would, one after the other. Run the checks: do the totals agree, do the claims match the evidence, do the records support the figures? Fix a mismatch at its source. Write a review and a next step. A pack whose numbers agree with each other is one you can defend.
